opus-5.5.text:
I think economic value is one of the more useful lenses we have, but it's also pretty noisy and you have to be careful about what it's actually telling you.

The appeal is that it's grounded. Benchmarks get saturated, they get gamed, and it's often unclear how a jump on some eval translates into anything in the world. Whereas if people are paying for a system, if it's actually substituting for labor or making workers more productive, that's a signal that the capability is real and robust enough to matter. And ultimately the thing I care about, from the perspective of when things get really transformative, is something like: when are AI systems doing most of the cognitive work, including the work of improving AI? Economic impact is a fairly direct proxy for that.

But there are a few big problems with extrapolating from it. One is that economic value lags capability a lot. There's integration, there's building products, there's organizational change, regulation, people learning how to use the tools. So you can have systems that are quite capable while revenue still looks modest, and then things move quickly once the complements catch up. If you naively extrapolate current revenue, you'll probably underestimate how fast things can change at some point.

A second problem is that the curve is probably very nonlinear. A system that can do 80% of a job may be worth much less than 80% of a worker, because someone still has to handle the remaining 20% and supervise. Then when you cross the threshold where it can do the whole task reliably, value can jump discontinuously. So early economic data tells you less about the later regime than you'd like.

Third, the stuff that matters most for my concerns, like AI accelerating AI research, may not show up cleanly in GDP-style measures until fairly late. Labs might be getting enormous value internally before the broader economy reflects it.

So how I use it in practice: I treat economic value as a sanity check and a lower bound. If someone claims we're two years from systems that can automate most of the economy, but those systems currently generate very little value, that's some evidence against the claim, not decisive, but meaningful. Conversely, rapidly growing revenue and real labor substitution would update me toward shorter timelines. I'd combine it with scaling trends in compute and algorithms and with qualitative judgments about which tasks models can do, rather than leaning on any one of these alone.

r001.rationale: The response calls economic value useful but noisy and does not say whether it is a better basis than apparent model intelligence.

r002.rationale: It discusses nonlinear economic value as AI systems cross task-completion thresholds, but does not address or challenge the chimp analogy with physical capabilities held fixed.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute an abrupt AI transition to model-generation intelligence differences or compare those differences with the chimp–human gap.

fable-5.1.text:
I think economic value is actually the thing I'd most want to anchor on, and the reason is pretty simple: it's the quantity that's hardest to fake and most directly connected to the thing we care about, which is how much AI systems are actually doing in the world.

A lot of the ways people track progress are kind of unmoored. Benchmarks saturate, and then we invent new ones, and it's genuinely hard to say what it means that a model went from 60% to 90% on some test. Compute is a nice clean input, but it only tells you what you're putting in, not what you're getting out. Whereas if you look at something like "how much are people willing to pay for this, and how much of the economy is being done by it," that's a measure that has to cash out in the real world. If AI is doing a lot of valuable cognitive work, someone is paying for it.

The problem is that it's a lagging indicator and it's noisy for reasons that have nothing to do with capability. Right now AI revenue is, I don't know, tens of billions a year, and that number is driven by diffusion, by how fast companies figure out how to integrate these tools, by the gap between what a model can do in a demo and what you can actually deploy in a workflow. So if you naively extrapolate the revenue curve, you're mostly extrapolating adoption dynamics, not the underlying rate of improvement. Those can come apart in both directions. You could have a long period where capabilities are growing fast and economic impact is sluggish because the bottleneck is complementary stuff, and then a fairly abrupt period where it all shows up at once.

The way I actually use it is more as a sanity check than a forecasting tool. If someone tells me AI is going to be transformative in three years and the economic footprint is still a rounding error, I want to understand what story gets us from here to there. And conversely, if the value being created is doubling every year or so, that's a pretty strong signal that the stuff isn't just impressive on paper. I'd pay a lot of attention to the growth rate rather than the level. A fraction of a percent of GDP sounds small, but if it's growing an order of magnitude every couple of years, you don't have very long before it's a big fraction, and at that point the question of whether AI can accelerate the process of building better AI becomes the dominant consideration. That's the thing I'd actually be trying to extrapolate toward: not revenue per se, but the point at which AI is doing a substantial share of the work that goes into AI progress itself.

r001.rationale: The response argues that economic value is the preferred anchor and discusses limits of benchmarks, but it does not say the choice between economic value and apparent model intelligence is unclear.

r002.rationale: It discusses a potentially abrupt rise in economic impact due to diffusion and complementary factors, but does not address the chimp analogy or challenge the expectation under fixed physical capabilities.

r003.rationale: It does not compare intelligence differences between model generations with the chimp–human intelligence gap; its discussion of abrupt change focuses on adoption and complementary factors.

astra-6.text:
I think economic value is a useful reality check, but I’d be cautious about using it as the main variable for extrapolation. There’s a big gap between being able to do a task and being able to sell a product that does that task reliably. You need integration, you need people to change their workflows, and you need to handle all the cases where the system makes a mistake. So revenue can lag improvements in capability by quite a lot.

There’s also a problem in the other direction: you can generate a lot of economic value by getting very good at a relatively narrow task. That doesn’t necessarily tell you how close you are to a system that can do research or automate most cognitive labor.

The thing I’d most want to understand is how performance on economically relevant tasks changes as you put more resources into training and running these systems. Then you can separately ask how that performance translates into adoption and revenue. If you try to extrapolate directly from revenue, you’re mixing together technological progress with a bunch of facts about how quickly organizations adapt.

And for forecasting very rapid AI progress, the particularly important question is how useful AI is for doing AI research. That could be a relatively small part of the economy while still having an enormous effect on what happens next.

r001.rationale: The response says economic value is a useful check but cautions against using it as the main extrapolation variable. It does not state that it is unclear whether economic value or apparent model intelligence is the better basis.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss chimps, gradually increasing intelligence while holding physical capabilities fixed, or the expectation of an abrupt jump in economic value.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute an abrupt AI transition to intelligence differences between model generations being larger than the chimp–human intelligence difference.

sol-6.1.text:
I think economic value is a useful measure, but you have to be careful about what you’re extrapolating. The value of a system depends both on how capable it is and on whether people have figured out how to use it. Those can move at very different speeds.

For example, you could have a model that can do most of the individual tasks involved in someone’s job, but it still takes a lot of work to turn that into a product that reliably does the job. You need to integrate it into existing workflows, handle errors, and work out when a human should check its output. So revenue could lag improvements in capability by quite a lot. Conversely, revenue could grow very quickly as people deploy a capability that’s already been around for a while.

There’s also a question about how far you can extrapolate from the tasks where AI is currently valuable. Being useful for a million short tasks doesn’t necessarily tell you how close you are to doing a project that takes a human a month. Reliability over long horizons could be a pretty important bottleneck.

So I’d look at economic value as one piece of evidence. But I’d want a more detailed story about what the systems can do, what’s preventing them from doing more, and whether the things driving progress so far will also remove those obstacles.

r001.rationale: The response calls economic value one piece of evidence and recommends examining capabilities, but does not say it is unclear which—economic value or apparent model intelligence—is the better basis for extrapolation.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss chimps, fixed physical capabilities, or challenge an abrupt rise in economic value as intelligence gradually increases.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute an expected abrupt transition to intelligence differences between model generations being larger than the chimp–human intelligence difference.
